title: throughput-contour-admission-notes
content:
Objective:
Provide a pragmatic, deployable admission and routing approach that keeps inference latency SLOs intact while maximizing useful throughput across regions and heterogeneous GPU pools. This doc introduces the "throughput contour" concept — a compact way to reason about admission using a small set of continuous signals (queue depth, GPU utilization, recent success rate) rather than brittle per-tenant heuristics.

Scope & constraints:
- Targets real-time text generation and chat endpoints where tail latency and token-cost are the primary concerns.
- Must operate with both local fast-path checks (sub-ms) and a slower global control-plane decisioning for cross-region reroutes.
- Support heterogeneous device performance (A100, H100, BFLOAT quantized variants) and model variants (full / quantized / distilled).
- Degraded networks and partial region outages expected; graceful fallback to other regions or lower-cost model variants mandatory.

Key signals we use (ranked by utility):
1) per-GPU util (15s rolling avg) — most immediate capacity indicator
2) local queue depth (per-worker queue length, 95th pct) — indicates short-term burst pressure
3) token processing rate (effective tokens/sec observed) — throughput achieved under current mix
4) recent rejection rate / timeouts — indicates whether backpressure is already active
5) warm cache hit rate (prefix/KV cache) — influences effective throughput and latency
6) per-route tail latency (p99) — SLO proximity metric

Throughput contour concept (overview):
- For each model variant and region we compute a small vector (contour) that maps observed GPU util -> safe throughput (tokens/sec). The contour can be represented as a few control points (low, medium, high util) and interpolated.
- Admission checks compare requested throughput (estimated tokens for the request) against the remaining headroom from the contour adjusted by short-term queue backpressure.
- Contours are continuously shaped by telemetry and a slow control-plane optimizer (every 30s–2m) that merges per-device statistics into region-level contours.

Admission decision flow (fast-path, local):
1) Parse request -> estimate token cost (model, length, temperature).
2) Lookup local contour for model-variant on this GPU pool. Apply a conservative scalar for p99 headroom (configurable, default 0.6).
3) Check local soft-credit bucket (continuous credit accumulator) for the pool. If credit >= estimated tokens and local queue_depth < local_queue_threshold, admit fast-path.
4) Otherwise mark request for slow-path routing (see below).

Soft-credit bucket semantics (lightweight token accounting):
- Each GPU pool maintains a credit balance measured in "tokens-equivalent". Credits replenish at a rate equal to contour-derived safe throughput (tokens/sec) scaled by pool weight. Credits are consumed by admitted requests.
- Credits decay slowly when pool is idling (to avoid burstiness) and are clipped at an upper bound to allow short bursts.
- Important: credits are a *hint* not a strict safety net — overloaded pools must still be able to stop accepting new work if latency SLOs break (see overload protection).

Slow-path / control-plane check (cross-region and fallback):
- Triggered when local bucket insufficient or queue depth high. Control-plane maintains a compact capacity cache with recent contours and a per-region health tag (green/yellow/red).
- Slow-path options: reroute to a compatible region, fall back to quantized/distilled model variant in same region, or enqueue with an expected wait-time if latency SLO permits.
- Reroute policy orders candidates by: health score, estimated additional network egress latency, and economic penalty (cost delta).

Overload detection & graceful degradation rules:
- If p99 latency > target for two consecutive evaluation windows, mark pool as degraded. Immediately reduce contour headroom and reduce replenishment rate of credits (aggressive shedding).
- Enforce priority lanes: control-plane assigns priority classes (best-effort, standard, premium). In overload, best-effort is shed first. For fairness, long-running requests get preemption markers so they are allowed to finish or be aborted according to policy.

Queue shaping and hedging: 
- Maintain per-worker short FIFO with a small skew buffer to reduce head-of-line latencies; use LIFO for premium lanes to minimize tail.
- Hedging: small probability (config per-route) of launching a hedged request on a warm warm-pool in the same region when p99 is approaching SLO and estimated token cost is high. Hedging is rate-limited and only used for premium traffic to control cost.

GPU utilization signal handling (practical notes):
- GPU util is noisy; smooth with an asymmetric EWMA that reacts faster to rising util and slower to falling util. Window ~15–30s.
- Combine util with queue depth to avoid false positives during transient microbursts caused by e.g., batching or cache warmups.
- Where direct GPU telemetry isn't available (private deployments), use proxy signals: running_process_count, average token time, dispatcher latencies.

Control-plane components and responsibilities:
- Regional Capacity Oracle: aggregates per-pool contours and publishes region-level contours and health tags. Runs lightweight optimizer that nudges contour control points based on recent observed throughput and tail-latency breaches.
- Global Router: consumes regional contours and makes cross-region decisions. Holds a small cache (TTL 15s) and falls back to deterministic hashing for cold paths to avoid thundering herd.
- Admission Supervisor: runs placement heuristics for slow-path work, enforces global priority budget, and records audit trail for decision explainability.

Metrics to track (minimum set):
- admitted/denied counts by route/model/region
- average refill_rate and credit_balance across pools
- queue depth distribution and 95/99 percentiles
- per-GPU util (avg/95/99) and contour control point history
- p50/p90/p99 latency by route and region
- reroute rate and successful cross-region fallbacks
- hedging invocations and their success improvement on p99

Runbook snippets (quick ops):
- If region p99 spikes and health=green -> check refill_rate trend. If refill_rate dropping, revert last contour optimizer change (control-plane keeps last N diffs).
- If many reroutes to a single target region -> that target is likely saturated; mark its health yellow and throttle reroutes for 60s.
- If GPU util shows sustained >95% and queue_depth rising -> scale up pool (if autoscaler available) else gradually reduce headroom and enable aggressive shedding for best-effort lanes.

Tuning experiments (suggested A/B tests):
- Compare fixed credit cap vs adaptive cap (cap as function of recent latency). Measure p99 and cost delta.
- Evaluate contour refresh intervals (15s vs 60s) for stability versus responsiveness tradeoffs.
- Hedging frequency sweep (0%, 1%, 5%) on premium routes to find knee of p99 improvement vs cost.

Known tradeoffs and failure modes:
- Overly aggressive contours reduce utilization (wasted GPU cycles) but protect latency. Conservative contours increase cost per successful token.
- Control-plane staleness: too infrequent updates lead to poor routing choices; too frequent updates risk oscillation. Add hysteresis and guardrails.
- Cold-start scenarios: region-level contours take time to warm. For small regions prefer conservative defaults and prefer cross-region routing for large requests until contour stabilizes.

Next steps / open questions:
- Formalize contour representation and serialization format (compact proto) for cross-region exchange.
- Integrate model-variant cost delta into contour math (allow optimizer to prefer quantized variants when headroom tight).
- Build a canary that applies 10% of traffic under the new fast-path soft-credit logic and records decision explainability metadata for analysis.

Appendix: example pseudocode (fast-path):
- estimate = estimate_tokens(request)
- contour = local_contour.lookup(model_variant)
- headroom = contour.safe_throughput_at(util_ewma) * headroom_scalar - queue_depth_penalty(queue_depth)
- if soft_credit.balance >= estimate and headroom >= estimate:
    admit_local()
  else:
    mark_slow_path()

Notes: this is intentionally lightweight and operational — not a formal math proof. The goal is to have a working implementation we can iterate on from telemetry and A/B experiments.
